CausalChain: CLDN18.2 is overexpressed on gastric cancer cells -> Tumor microenvironment becomes acidic and hypoxic, impairing immune cell function -> CLDN18.2-targeted CAR-T cells in this environment exhibit limited persistence and cytotoxicity -> Enhancing glycolytic capacity of CAR-T cells improves energy production under acidic/hypoxic conditions -> Metabolically reprogrammed CAR-T cells maintain function and persistence -> Enhanced tumor cell lysis and therapeutic outcomes in gastric cancer.
Hypothesis: Engineering CLDN18.2-specific CAR-T cells with enhanced glycolytic capacity will improve their persistence and cytotoxic activity in the acidic tumor microenvironment of gastric cancer, thereby augmenting therapeutic efficacy.
Abstract: Gastric cancer often exhibits aberrant expression of Claudin-18.2 (CLDN18.2), making this tight junction protein an attractive target for immunotherapeutic strategies. However, the hostile tumor microenvironment—characterized by acidity, hypoxia, and immunosuppressive cytokines—can impair the function and persistence of CLDN18.2‐targeted immune cells such as chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR‐T) cells. In this study, we propose that metabolic reprogramming of CLDN18.2‐targeted CAR‐T cells to enhance glycolytic capacity will improve their resilience in the acidic and nutrient‐deprived tumor milieu, resulting in enhanced antitumor efficacy in gastric cancer. This hypothesis is based on evidence that conventional CLDN18.2 targeting agents demonstrate antitumor activity, yet their effectiveness is potentially limited by the metabolic barriers inherent in solid tumors. This work provides a novel direction for improving cellular immunotherapy in gastric cancer by integrating metabolic adaptation strategies.
